1: Lectures seven and eight. Numerical and categorical variables, comparing non graphical and graphical exploratory analysis. We will apply every technique to every feature of one large real dataset, the Superstore Retail Orders, with eight thousand three hundred ninety nine rows and twenty one columns.
2: Meet the dataset. It has eight thousand three hundred ninety nine real retail orders for office supplies, technology and furniture, with sales, discount and shipping detail. We chose it because everyone understands buying something online: the price, the discount, the shipping cost, and whether the seller made a profit. It is also not a common teaching dataset like Titanic or Iris, so most students have never analysed it. Today's structure is to separate non graphical, or statistical, analysis from graphical, or visual, analysis, apply both to every feature, then compare what each one tells us. The principle: numbers first for precision, plots second for shape, and then always check that the two agree.
3: The numerical features are six. Sales is the total dollar value of the order. Profit is the dollar profit or loss, and it can be negative. Discount is the discount rate, from zero to about twenty five percent. Order quantity is the number of units, from one to fifty. Unit price is the price of one unit before discount. Shipping cost is the dollar cost of shipping the order.
4: The categorical features are three. Product category has three clean groups: office supplies, technology and furniture. Ship mode is regular air, delivery truck or express air, which tells us how the order was shipped. Customer segment is consumer, corporate, home office or small business, which tells us who placed the order. Together they describe what was bought, how it shipped and who bought it, the three natural ways to slice any retail order.
5: Non graphical technique zero: the missing value check. It simply counts how many cells in each column are empty. It is the very first non graphical check on any dataset, before any statistic or plot. At scale it is one line, df dot isna dot sum, which checks every column at once.
6: The result: only product base margin has missing values, sixty three orders or point seven five percent, a small, easily flagged gap. Every one of the six numerical features we use today has zero missing values, and so do all the categorical features we use.
7: Part one: non graphical, or statistical, exploratory analysis. Numbers first: central tendency, dispersion and shape, applied to every numerical feature before we look at a single plot.
8: Technique one: central tendency. The mean is the arithmetic average and is sensitive to extreme values. The median is the middle value when sorted and resists extremes. The mode is the most frequent value. In pandas, df of num cols dot mean, dot median and dot mode each compute their statistic for every numerical feature in one line, with no loop.
9: Results for central tendency. Profit shows the most dramatic gap: the mean is one hundred eighty one dollars and eighteen cents, but the median is minus one dollar fifty. The average and the typical order tell opposite stories. Order quantity and discount have mean and median close together, consistent with their flat, even shapes. Sales and unit price both have a mean far above the median, a first non graphical hint of strong right skew.
10: Technique two: dispersion. Standard deviation is how far values typically spread from the mean. Range is maximum minus minimum, and is sensitive to a single extreme value. The I Q R, Q three minus Q one, is the spread of the middle fifty percent and resists extremes. Again it is the same one line pattern, df of num cols dot std, for every feature at once.
11: Results for dispersion. For sales, the standard deviation of three thousand five hundred eighty five is more than twice its I Q R of fifteen hundred sixty six, a strong signal that a handful of very large orders are stretching the spread. Profit's standard deviation, eleven ninety seven, is over four times its I Q R of two forty six, the same pattern for gains and losses. Order quantity's standard deviation and I Q R are in a sensible proportion, which is typical, well behaved dispersion.
12: Technique three: shape, meaning skewness and kurtosis. Skewness of zero means symmetric, positive means a long right tail, and the further from zero, the more lopsided. Kurtosis measures how heavy the tails are. A very high kurtosis means extreme values are far more common than a normal distribution predicts. Again, df of num cols dot skew and dot kurtosis give them for every feature in one line.
13: Results for shape. Unit price is extraordinarily skewed, fourteen point one three, with a kurtosis of two seventy one, the most extreme feature in the dataset. Sales, skew five point three nine, and profit, skew three point six five, are also dramatically skewed, though less than unit price. Order quantity, skew minus point zero two, and discount, skew point zero seven, sit almost exactly at zero. They are genuinely symmetric.
14: This ranks skewness across every feature. Unit price towers over everything else, on a scale so extreme it barely fits on the same chart. Order quantity and discount sit right at zero, the two most symmetric features. At this point the numbers alone tell us that sales, profit and unit price are wildly skewed, but they cannot show us what that shape looks like. For that we need pictures.
15: Part two: graphical exploratory analysis of numerical variables. Now we turn every one of those numbers into a picture: histogram, density, boxplot and violin plot, for all six numerical features.
16: Plot type one: the histogram. It splits the range of a variable into bins and counts how many rows fall in each bin, the most direct picture of a distribution's shape. Tall bars mean common values, and the overall shape, symmetric, skewed or multi peaked, tells you how the data behaves. It is best for a first, honest look at any numerical column before computing statistics.
17: Here are histograms for all six features. Order quantity and discount show flat, evenly spread bars across their whole range, visual confirmation of their near zero skewness. Sales, unit price and shipping cost show one towering bar near zero and an almost invisible tail, the picture behind their extreme skewness numbers. Profit shows a sharp spike near zero with real mass on both the negative and positive side, visually confirming the loss making orders we found earlier.
18: Plot type two: the density plot, also called K D E, or kernel density estimation. It is a smoothed version of a histogram, a continuous curve instead of discrete bars. It removes the arbitrary choice of bin width, giving a cleaner, more stable picture of the underlying shape. The trade off is that smoothing can hide small real spikes that a histogram shows clearly, so the two plot types complement each other.
19: Density plots for all six features. Order quantity's curve confirms a genuinely flat, close to uniform shape. Profit's curve shows a sharp, narrow peak straddling zero, visually distinct from the one sided skew of sales or unit price. Sales and unit price again collapse into a flat line squashed against zero. Density plots handle moderate skew well, but not this level of it.
20: Plot type three: the boxplot. It shows five numbers in one compact picture: minimum, Q one, median, Q three and maximum, plus individually plotted outlier points. The box spans the middle fifty percent, the I Q R. The whiskers extend to the normal range, and dots beyond them are flagged outliers. It is best for comparing spread and spotting outliers at a glance, especially across several features side by side.
21: Boxplots for all six features. Order quantity and discount show honest, well formed boxes with essentially no outliers. Profit's box straddles zero and has outlier dots stretching in both directions: large losses on one side, large gains on the other. Sales, unit price and shipping cost all show a box crushed toward zero, exactly matching what their dispersion numbers already warned us about.
22: Plot type four: the violin plot. It mirrors a density curve on both sides of a central boxplot, so you see the full distribution shape and the five number summary together. A boxplot alone can hide whether the data is single peaked, multi peaked or lopsided, and a violin reveals that shape directly. It is best when the shape itself, not just the median and spread, is part of the story.
23: Violin plots for all six features. Order quantity has the most rectangular, even violin body, the clearest visual confirmation of its uniform shape. Profit's violin is narrow and symmetric around zero, unlike the one sided needles of sales or unit price. Sales, unit price and shipping cost again appear as needle thin spikes. The violin plot cannot rescue a shape this extreme, any more than the density plot could.
24: Plot type five: distribution comparisons. This overlays the same numerical feature's density curve for several categories on one plot. Curves that overlap heavily mean the category barely affects that feature. Curves that separate mean the category is a real driver of it. It is best as an early, visual check of whether a categorical feature is worth investigating further as a predictor.
25: Here is profit compared across product category, shown between minus two thousand and two thousand dollars. All three categories are centred close to zero, with both gains and losses in every category. Technology shows a visibly wider spread than office supplies or furniture: bigger wins and bigger losses. The average profit confirms this. Technology averages four hundred twenty nine dollars per order, more than six times furniture's sixty eight dollars.
26: Here is shipping cost compared across ship mode, as violin plots. Delivery truck shows the widest spread and the highest typical shipping cost. Regular air and express air both cluster at lower costs, with express air slightly higher. This is an expected, sensible pattern: heavier or bulkier shipments that need truck delivery naturally cost more to ship.
27: Part three: non graphical versus graphical. We now put the numbers and the pictures side by side, to see where they agree and what each one uniquely reveals.
28: First comparison: unit price. The non graphical statistics said: skewness of fourteen point one three, the most extreme of any feature; kurtosis of two seventy one; a mean of eighty nine dollars, more than four times the median of twenty one; and ten percent of rows flagged as outliers. The graphical plots showed: a histogram with one towering bar near zero and everything else invisible; a boxplot crushed flat with a dense wall of outlier dots reaching past sixty seven hundred dollars; and a violin that is an almost perfectly straight needle. Combined inference: most items are inexpensive, but a small set of high end products pull every average sharply upward.
29: Second comparison: order quantity. The numbers said: skewness of minus point zero two, essentially symmetric; mean and median almost on top of each other; kurtosis of minus one point two one, flatter tailed than a normal distribution; and zero percent outliers. The plots showed: an evenly spread, almost rectangular histogram across the full one to fifty range; a wide, honest box with no outlier dots; and the most rectangular violin of any feature. Combined inference: the number and the picture agree closely, a rare, reassuring case in this dataset.
30: The overall lesson. When they agree, as with order quantity, the numbers and plots tell the same story, and you can trust either technique alone. When they diverge in detail, as with unit price, the skewness number correctly warned of extreme skew, but only the boxplot showed that the entire spread lives in the outlier dots, not in the box. The practical rule: non graphical statistics are fast and precise but abstract, graphical plots are intuitive but can hide detail behind smoothing or scale, so always use both together. The numbers tell you something is unusual. The plot tells you what it looks like and why.
31: Part four: categorical variables. We apply every plot type, frequency table, bar plot and pie chart, to all three categorical features of the same large dataset.
32: Plot type six: the frequency table. It is a simple count, and percentage, of how many rows fall into each category, the categorical equivalent of describe for a number. The biggest number tells you the most common category, and a category with a tiny count is a warning sign for later grouped analysis. It is the very first check on any categorical column.
33: Frequency tables for all three categorical features. Product category: office supplies is the majority with four thousand six hundred ten orders, fifty four point nine percent, and furniture is the smallest with seventeen twenty four, twenty point five percent. Ship mode: regular air dominates with six thousand two seventy orders, seventy four point seven percent, and express air is rarest, eleven point seven percent. Customer segment: corporate is the largest at thirty six point six percent, and the other three are fairly close together.
34: Plot type seven: the bar plot. It turns a frequency table into a picture, one bar per category, with height equal to the count or another summary statistic. The eye compares bar heights far faster than numbers in a table. It is best for presenting a frequency table visually, or comparing a summary like average profit across categories.
35: Bar plots for all three categorical features. Product category shows office supplies towering over the other two. Ship mode shows a steep drop after regular air, because most orders default to standard shipping. Customer segment shows a real but modest lead for corporate over the other three, which are fairly even.
36: Plot type eight: the pie chart. It divides a whole into proportional slices, a part to whole view instead of a side by side comparison. A caution: pie charts get hard to read past four or five slices, and they are poor for comparing two similar sized slices precisely. They are best for a small number of categories where the part to whole framing is the point. Product category, with exactly three groups, fits well. Region, with eight categories, is better as a bar plot.
37: Here is the product category mix as a pie chart. Office supplies alone accounts for well over half of every order placed. Technology and furniture together still make up less than half of the pie. Seeing this as a part to whole picture makes office supplies' dominance easier to feel at a glance than the bar plot alone.
38: Part five: detecting anomalies. We combine the non graphical I Q R rule with the graphical boxplots we already saw, and connect outliers back to the profit finding.
39: The method. Compute Q one, Q three and I Q R equals Q three minus Q one. Flag anything below Q one minus one point five times I Q R, or above Q three plus one point five times I Q R, as an outlier. This is a non graphical rule with a graphical twin: the exact same fences are what a boxplot draws as whiskers. They are two views of one idea. And not every outlier is an error: a twenty seven thousand dollar profit order and a minus fourteen thousand dollar loss are both genuine, correctly recorded business events, not data mistakes.
40: Applying the method to all six features. Profit has one thousand seven hundred four outliers, twenty point three percent of rows, the highest rate, capturing both large gains and large losses. Sales has one thousand forty two, twelve point four percent. Shipping cost and unit price have eleven point six and ten point one percent. Discount has just three outliers, and order quantity has none, the tamest feature in the dataset. The business connection: profit's outliers are not noise. They are exactly the extreme wins and losses that matter for understanding why fifty point eight percent of orders lose money.
41: Recap of lectures seven and eight. We applied non graphical techniques, mean, median, mode, standard deviation, I Q R, skewness and kurtosis, and graphical techniques, histogram, density, boxplot, violin and distribution comparison, to every one of the six numerical features. In total, eight plot types and three families of non graphical technique were covered, matching every result with its plot and every plot with its number. Order quantity and discount behave normally by every measure. Sales, profit and unit price share one extreme story, confirmed by both approaches. The numbers flag that something is unusual, and the plots show exactly what and why.
42: Any questions? Next up: correlation, covariance and scatterplots, in lectures nine and ten.
